---
title: "Tutorial: Responsible use of large language models"
format: html
---

Large language models (LLMs), like GPT, are powerful tools for generating text that can be used for coding, report writing, data analysis, and much more.
This is at once empowering (LLMs are powerful and can save you time!) and risky (LLMs can make mistakes that are hard to detect).
Moreover, reliance on LLMs can lead to weakening of your own skills and understanding, which undermines the very purpose of education.

LLMs are powerful tools that you will encounter and use when you leave this class, so it's important to learn how to use them responsibly and effectively.
As described in the [syllabus](../syllabus.qmd#sec-llm), you are generally permitted to use LLMs in this course, but ultimately, you are responsible for guaranteeing, understanding, and interpreting your results, and you can't do this if you don't understand the code that you are running (this isn't exclusive to code generated by LLMs -- it also applies to code that you copy from the internet!).
Assessment will focus on understanding, expressed through activities that are not readily amenable to LLM use, so using LLMs to do your homework for you will not lead to good grades, but you are free to explore ways to use LLMs to improve your fundamental understanding.

Things are changing quickly, and the landscape of LLMs is evolving rapidly.
Rather than provide a lesson plan for you, this page will provide some resources for self-learning.
If you have suggestions for additional resources, please let me know!

## Links and resources

* [GitHub Copilot](https://github.com/features/copilot){target=_blank} is an extension for VS Code that can provide suggestions for code completion and editing. It is [free](https://techcommunity.microsoft.com/t5/educator-developer-blog/step-by-step-setting-up-github-student-and-github-copilot-as-an/ba-p/3736279){target=_blank} for students and educators.
* [Blog: "Bob Carpenter thinks GPT-4 is awesome"](https://statmodeling.stat.columbia.edu/2023/08/20/bob-carpenter-thinks-gpt-4-is-awesome/){target=_blank}: this post highlights how GPT-4 is able to write a program in Stan, a statistical programming language, and also the mistakes that it makes. Finding and correcting these mistakes requires knowing the Stan language and having a deep understanding of the statistical model, but someone with this expertise could potentially use GPT-4 to accelerate their coding workflow. The comments are also interesting and insightful.
* [AI Snake Oil](https://www.aisnakeoil.com/){target=_blank} is a blog that seeks to dispel hype, remove misconceptions, and clarify the limits of AI. The authors are in the Princeton University Department of Computer Science.
* [Everyone is Cheating Their Way Through College](https://archive.ph/qIXd0) is a long-form article that discusses some of the ways that students are using LLMs to cheat and underscores the need to rethink the goals of education and how we measure whether we are achieving those goals.
